title: AI May Change the World. It Just Won’t Change How You Invest | Dimensional
gist: Dimensional founder David Booth argues AI may transform the economy but won't help investors beat efficient markets, since any information edge is shared by all and no AI model will reliably pick winners. Citing the 1999 telecom leaders (only 1 of the top 20 survived intact), he urges a broadly diversified buy-and-hold portfolio over concentrated AI-stock bets.

insights.claim: David Booth argues AI may be an 'ice block to refrigerator' level advance for society but will not change how prices get set in stock and bond markets.
insights.speaker: David Booth
insights.so_what: Do not expect AI tools to create a durable stock-picking edge; keep process rooted in market-price efficiency.
insights.quote: But one thing I’m confident it won’t do is change how prices get set in stock and bond markets.

themes.theme: Betting on AI winners is risky

insights.claim: Concentrating a portfolio in 'AI stocks' could lead to disappointment because most companies will likely use AI to improve efficiency and productivity, so the benefits will not be confined to obvious AI names.
insights.speaker: David Booth
insights.so_what: Avoid overconcentration in AI-themed names; AI productivity gains may accrue across many sectors.

insights.claim: Of the top 20 US telecom stock market performance contributors in 1999 (led by Lucent Technologies and Nextel Comms), only 1 survived in its corporate structure twenty-five years later, per Dimensional/CRSP data.
insights.speaker: David Booth
insights.so_what: The dot-com telecom buildout is a cautionary analog for today's AI infrastructure leaders: early leaders often do not survive.
insights.locator: Many have compared today’s investing environment

insights.claim: Booth expects some of today's AI market leaders to thrive, others to fail, and entirely new, currently undiscussed winners to emerge, noting Google did not go public until 2004 and Levi Strauss was a big winner of the Gold Rush.
insights.speaker: David Booth
insights.so_what: The eventual AI winners may be indirect or not yet public, so thematic picks in current leaders may miss them.
insights.quote: Some of today’s market leaders will thrive. Others won’t.

insights.claim: Hyperscaler AI capital spending is expected to exceed $1.2 trillion in 2027 on data centers, chips and more (citing a Goldman estimate of a 50% rise), but Booth says the beneficiaries might be Big Tech or another sector entirely.
insights.speaker: David Booth
insights.so_what: Massive AI capex is a known quantity; who captures its returns is not, arguing for broad rather than concentrated exposure.

insights.claim: Booth recommends owning public markets through a broadly diversified buy-and-hold portfolio that includes AI stocks and many others, so investors participate in whatever the future becomes rather than betting on what they think it will become.
insights.speaker: David Booth
insights.so_what: Broad index-like exposure captures AI winners automatically without needing to identify them.

insights.claim: Public markets finance thousands of competing ideas, tolerate spectacular failures, and move capital rapidly toward what works, which lets ordinary people, not just founders, VCs and insiders, share in innovation's wealth creation without overconcentration risk.
insights.speaker: David Booth
insights.so_what: Public-market diversification is a democratized way to capture innovation upside versus concentrated private bets.
